references.text: Jesus forgives the paralyzed man's sins, and the scribes ask who can forgive sins but God alone – the same theme of Jesus' authority to forgive sins.
The preceding verse where Jesus explains that her many sins are forgiven because she loved much, which leads directly to the declaration of forgiveness in verse 48.
The reaction from the guests asking, "Who is this who even forgives sins?" – as well as Jesus' words to the woman that her faith has saved her. Shows the context and consequences of forgiveness.
Jesus says to the paralyzed man: "Be of good cheer, son; your sins are forgiven you." The same wording and authority to declare sins forgiven.
Jesus says to the paralyzed man: "Your sins are forgiven you" and defends his right to forgive sins before the scribes. A parallel to Jesus' authority over forgiveness of sins.
God says: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and your sins I will not remember." Old Testament background for God's forgiveness of sin – a right that Jesus here exercises.
"Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered." The Old Testament promise of blessing connected to forgiveness of sins, which Jesus fulfills here.
Micah praises God who forgives sin and casts all sins into the depths of the sea – prophetic background for the forgiveness that Jesus declares.
Paul preaches forgiveness of sins through Jesus – apostolic continuation of Jesus' authority to declare forgiveness of sins.
In Christ we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins. A theological elaboration on the forgiveness that Jesus personally declares in Luke 7:48.
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous, so that he forgives us our sins." Confirms God's faithful forgiveness of sin, in line with Jesus' declaration.
